chunks: And Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allāh narrated this hadith from Jamīl ibn Ṣāliḥ and Ḥammād ibn ʿUthmān, from ʿUmar ibn Yazīd: similarly to that.

Its meaning is that if she saw the greater fluid during her sleep, then when she awakens she does not see anything, then ghusl (ritual bath) is not obligatory upon her. And that which indicates what we have said...

key_terms.الْحَدِيثَ: the hadith being transmitted and explained
key_terms.الْغُسْلُ: ghusl (ritual bath), the obligatory purification being discussed
key_terms.الْمَاءَ الْأَعْظَمَ: the greater fluid seen in sleep, referring contextually to the cause associated with janabah
key_terms.انْتَبَهَتْ: she awoke, marking the point at which the ruling is determined
key_terms.حَالِ مَنَامِهَا: the state of her sleep, indicating that the experience occurred during sleep
key_terms.لَا يَجِبُ: is not obligatory, expressing the legal conclusion

ai.seo_question: Does ghusl (ritual bath) become obligatory if a woman sees discharge in a dream but finds nothing upon waking?
ai.summary: This passage gives a legal ruling concerning janabah and ghusl (ritual bath). It states that if a woman sees such a dream in sleep but, upon waking, finds no trace of fluid, then ghusl is not obligatory upon her.
